Q: Does migration to server side GTM always involve creation of a new GA4 property? A:

No, you don't need a new GA4 property , and I'd actually advise against it.

The key insight missing from the other answers: you don't need to migrate individual GA4 Event tags at all.

How it actually works:

Set transport_url once on your GA4 Configuration tag pointing to your sGTM endpoint:

transport_url → https://gtm.yourdomain.com

That's it. All your existing GA4 Event tags in the web container will automatically route through sGTM — no individual tag changes needed.

On the server side, the GA4 Client handles GA4 hits natively out of the box. You only need to create a single GA4 tag in the server container to forward events to your existing Measurement ID.

About creating a new GA4 property:

The official docs suggest this as a "safe" option, but in practice it creates more work, not less. You'd need to:

  • Duplicate all your custom event tags in the server container

  • Recreate all custom dimensions and metrics from scratch

  • Run two properties in parallel and reconcile data

If you're confident in your setup (and sGTM Preview makes it easy to validate before publishing), migrate directly to your existing property. That's the standard approach for anyone with solid sGTM experience.

The only scenario where a new property makes sense is if you want a clean baseline comparison — but for a straightforward infrastructure migration, it's unnecessary overhead.

Validation checklist before publishing:

  • Confirm client_id is being parsed correctly from the _ga cookie in sGTM Preview

  • Check GA4 DebugView with sGTM Preview active to verify events land correctly

  • If using Consent Mode v2, verify consent_state is forwarded properly

Q: How to make gtm.js SPFX integration work with the new Content Security Policy (CSP)? A:

The problem is not with the GTM setup itself — it's with how the script is being injected. Here is what's happening and how to fix it.

The fix

Use SPComponentLoader.loadScript() to load GTM directly as an external script from within your Application Customizer. This is the CSP-compliant equivalent of what the classic GTM snippet does manually — without any innerHTML or document.createElement.

Step 1 — Register GTM's domain in SharePoint Admin Center (one-time admin step)

Navigate to SharePoint Admin Center → Advanced → Script sources → Add source and add:

https://www.googletagmanager.com

This step is required because SPComponentLoader.loadScript() loads scripts dynamically at runtime, and SharePoint does not auto-trust those domains the way it does scripts bundled inside your .sppkg. Wildcards like *.googletagmanager.com are not supported — the exact origin is required.

Step 2 — Replace the injection code in your Application Customizer

Remove the .js file approach, the document.createElement calls, and all innerHTML assignments. Replace with the following inside your customizer's onInit:

import { override } from '@microsoft/decorators';
import { BaseApplicationCustomizer } from '@microsoft/sp-application-base';
import { SPComponentLoader } from '@microsoft/sp-loader';

const GTM_ID: string = 'GTM-XXXX'; // replace with your container ID

export default class GtmInjectorApplicationCustomizer
  extends BaseApplicationCustomizer<{}> {

  @override
  public async onInit(): Promise<void> {

    // Prevent duplicate injection if the customizer fires more than once
    if ((window as any).__gtmLoaded) return Promise.resolve();
    (window as any).__gtmLoaded = true;

    // Initialize dataLayer before gtm.js loads — same as the standard GTM snippet
    (window as any).dataLayer = (window as any).dataLayer || [];
    (window as any).dataLayer.push({
      'gtm.start': new Date().getTime(),
      event: 'gtm.js'
    });

    // Load GTM as a trusted external script — no innerHTML, no inline scripting
    await SPComponentLoader.loadScript(
      `https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js?id=${GTM_ID}`
    );

    // Track initial page view
    this._pushPageView();

    // SharePoint Modern is a SPA — hook into navigation events
    // so subsequent page transitions are tracked without a full reload
    this.context.application.navigatedEvent.add(this, () => this._pushPageView());
    window.addEventListener('popstate', () => this._pushPageView());

    return Promise.resolve();
  }

  private _pushPageView(): void {
    (window as any).dataLayer.push({
      event: 'page_view',
      page_path: window.location.pathname,
      page_title: document.title,
      page_location: window.location.href
    });
  }
}

Your GTM container configuration does not need to change at all — only the injection method changes.

Step 3 — Remove the <noscript> body snippet

Since the customizer runs through JavaScript, the <noscript> block would only fire when JavaScript is entirely disabled — at which point the customizer itself would not have run either. It is safe to leave it out, and avoids a potential CSP frame-src violation from the GTM iframe.

Verifying the fix

Append ?csp=enforce to any Modern SharePoint page URL with the solution deployed, then open DevTools (F12) → Console. If GTM fires correctly in GTM Preview mode and no Content Security Policy errors appear, the setup is complete.

To audit CSP violations across your tenant, go to Microsoft Purview → Audit and search for the activity Violated Content Security Policy.

Why the hosted .js file approach did not work

The sequence of what was happening:

Step What happened CSP result
SPComponentLoader loads your .js file from the document library File fetched from whitelisted domain Allowed
Your .js sets gtmScript.innerHTML = '<script>...</script>' Inline script injection Blocked — unsafe-inline
The inner GTM snippet tries to dynamically create another <script> element Dynamic script creation from inline context Blocked — unsafe-eval

Whitelisting a file only covers fetching that file. It does not grant that file permission to inject further inline scripts downstream.

Which SPFx script loading patterns are auto-trusted vs manual

Pattern Auto-trusted by SharePoint?
Scripts bundled in .sppkg (deployed to ClientSideAssets) Yes
cdnBasePath declared in write-manifests.json Yes
Libraries declared in externals in config.json Yes
SPComponentLoader.loadScript() at runtime No — manual Admin Center registration required
Inline <script> / innerHTML / document.createElement with content Blocked entirely — no workaround available

Reference

  • Support for Content Security Policy (CSP) in SharePoint Online — Microsoft Learn — covers all SPFx script loading patterns and which ones require manual trust registration.
  • SharePoint Online CSP Enforcement Dates and Guidance — Microsoft Community Hub
  • Github Reference - https://github.com/pnp/sp-dev-fx-extensions/pull/1820

Q: The right square bracket within a charlist in the LIKE statement in Microsoft Access A:

In Regular Expressions the right square bracket ] can be escaped by preceeding it with the backslash \, so \] matches ]. But documentation for Regular Expressions is not updated any more, what is suspicious, for example: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/internet-explorer/ie-developer/scripting-articles/ms974570(v=msdn.10)?redirectedfrom=MSDN . Is it deprecated ?

Here is an example function:

Else: Exit Function

If RE Is Nothing Then
    Set RE = New RegExp
    'Set RE = CreateObject("VBScript.RegExp")

        .IgnoreCase = True
        .Global = True

        .Pattern = Pattern

str = Nz(Fld)

Perhaps it could be written better. And such custom function is much slower then direct Like statement in a query.

Q: How to prevent Prettier from moving comments to new line A:

This behaviour is not configurable, but there is a way.

  • Put that file into .prettierignore
  • or use block-suppressing comments in front of the affected block
  // prettier-ignore
  const login = useCallback(async (values: LoginFormValues) => {
    await loginMutation.mutateAsync(values)
    await meQuery.refetch()
  }, [loginMutation.mutateAsync, meQuery.refetch]) // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
